title: Caching
summary: Keep a copy of expensive answers close by, so you rarely redo the expensive work. The cheapest way to make systems fast — and the source of subtle staleness bugs.

blocks.markdown:
A cache is a small, fast store of copies, checked before the slow source of truth.

- **Hit** = found in cache (fast). **Miss** = not there; fetch from source and usually populate.
- Works because of **locality** — a small **hot set** of keys serves most traffic.
- The core trade-off is **speed vs freshness**: a cache can serve **stale** data.
- The headline metric is **hit ratio** — a small drop multiplies database load.

blocks.subTitle: Which tool
blocks.markdown:
Match the cache to the job.

| Situation | Reach for |
|---|---|
| Read-heavy app you control | Cache-aside + Redis |
| Simplest, fastest blob cache | Memcached |
| Data structures, persistence, pub/sub | Redis |
| Static assets, global users | CDN |
| Write must never be stale | Write-through |

blocks.subTitle: Layered hierarchy
blocks.markdown:
Data passes through several caches, each closer to the user and checked first.

![Cache layers from browser to database](assets/caching/cache-layers.svg)

- **Browser cache** — free, per user.
- **CDN edge** — static content from a nearby city.
- **In-process cache** — server RAM; fast but not shared.
- **Distributed cache (Redis)** — shared across servers, one network hop.
- **Database** — paid only on a full miss.

The closer the copy, the faster it is — and the more you must worry about staleness.

assets.alt: Cache layers from browser to database

blocks.subTitle: Reads: cache-aside
blocks.markdown:
**Cache-aside** is the default read path: the app owns the miss logic.

```python
def get(key):
    v = cache.get(key)
    if v is not None:
        return v              # hit
    v = db.read(key)          # miss -> source
    cache.set(key, v, ttl)    # populate for next time
    return v
```

- First read of any key always misses (**cold cache**).
- **Read-through** moves this logic into the cache layer — same loop, the cache owns the miss.

blocks.subTitle: Write strategies
blocks.markdown:
When data changes, how the write touches cache vs database is a speed/safety trade.

![Write-through, write-back, write-around](assets/caching/write-strategies.svg)

- **Write-through** — cache + DB synchronously. Always fresh, slower writes.
- **Write-back** — cache now, DB later async. Fastest, but **loses data** if the node dies first.
- **Write-around** — DB only, cache fills on later read miss.

Common pattern: write the DB, then **delete** the key (not update) so the next read repopulates fresh.

blocks.subTitle: Eviction
blocks.markdown:
A cache is small on purpose, so a full cache evicts to make room — throw out what you're least likely to need.

- **LRU** — evict least-recently-used. The cheap, sensible default.
- **LFU** — evict least-frequently-used. Good when popularity is stable.
- **W-TinyLFU** — modern admission via a frequency sketch; beats LRU under skewed load. Cite this for "better than LRU."
- **TTL** — a lifespan, not a policy; layer it on top so nothing lives forever.

blocks.subTitle: Invalidation
blocks.markdown:
Invalidation is the hard part: the source changed, so cached copies may be wrong.

- **TTL expiry** — let entries time out. Simple; accepts staleness up to the window.
- **Explicit** — delete affected keys on write. Precise, but you must know every key.
- **Versioned keys** — bake a version in (`user:42:v7`); bump it to invalidate.
- **Event-based** — changes publish events that evict everywhere.

**Delete, don't update** — deletes are idempotent and avoid concurrent-write races.

blocks.subTitle: Distributed caching
blocks.markdown:
Spread the cache over many nodes — but which node holds which key?

- `node = hash(key) % N` is a **trap**: change N and almost every key remaps, flooding the DB.
- **Consistent hashing** places nodes and keys on a ring; only ~1/N of keys move when membership changes. **Virtual nodes** even out load.
- **Hot key** — one key (a viral post) melts a single node. Fix by replicating it, fronting it with a local cache, or splitting the value.

blocks.subTitle: Three classic failures
blocks.markdown:
All three are misses ganging up on the database.

![Cache stampede: many requests miss and hit the DB together](assets/caching/stampede.svg)

- **Stampede** — a hot key expires; thousands rebuild it at once. Fix: single-flight lock, stale-while-revalidate, jittered TTLs.
- **Penetration** — requests for keys that don't exist. Fix: negative cache + Bloom filter.
- **Avalanche** — many keys expire together (or cold restart). Fix: TTL jitter, warm-up, circuit breakers.

assets.alt: Cache stampede: many requests miss and hit the DB together

blocks.subTitle: What you're trading
blocks.markdown:
Caching is a handful of dials.

- **Freshness vs load** — longer TTL = higher hit ratio but more staleness.
- **Durability vs write speed** — write-back is fast but loses data; write-through is durable but slow.
- **Memory vs hit ratio** — diminishing returns; 90%→95% costs far more RAM than 50%→70%.
- **Local vs distributed** — in-process is fastest but per-server; distributed is shared but a network hop.

blocks.subTitle: Rules of thumb
blocks.markdown:
Default moves that cover most cases.

- Read-heavy, tolerates seconds of staleness → **cache-aside + TTL**.
- Writes can't be stale/lost → **write-through**, or don't cache that path.
- A few very hot keys → **local cache in front of the distributed one**.
- Flooded by nonexistent keys → **negative caching + Bloom filter**.
- Expiry spiking the DB → **TTL jitter + stale-while-revalidate** before adding nodes.

blocks.subTitle: Real systems
blocks.markdown:
The caches you'll actually reach for.

- **Redis** — in-memory data structures, persistence, pub/sub, clustering; single-threaded per command (atomic). Pick it when you need more than key→value.
- **Memcached** — minimal, multi-threaded blob cache, LRU. Pick it for the simplest, fastest look-aside.
- **CDN** — global edge cache for static assets; cuts ~150 ms cross-continent to ~10–30 ms.
- **Meta's memcache** — leases stop stampedes; delete-on-write; cross-region invalidation. The lesson: *invalidation, not speed, is the hard part.*

blocks.subTitle: Why hit ratio dominates
blocks.markdown:
Misses are what cost you — protecting hit ratio is the whole game.

Service at 10k reads/s, DB caps ~2k/s. **DB load = reads × (1 − hit ratio)**:

- **90% hit** → 1,000 misses/s. Safe.
- **80% hit** → 2,000 misses/s. At the cliff.
- **70% hit** → 3,000 misses/s. Overloaded.

A 10-point drop *doubled* DB load. **Avg latency** = hit%×hit + miss%×miss; at 90% that's 0.9×1 + 0.1×10 = **1.9 ms** vs 10 ms uncached.

The mistakes that bite:

- **"The cache is the source of truth."** It isn't — the DB is. If the system breaks when the cache is empty, that's a bug.
- **"Caching makes everything faster."** Only hits. A miss is slightly *slower* than no cache.
- **"Update the cache on every write."** Races leave stale values — delete instead.
- **"`hash % N` is fine."** It mass-remaps on any membership change — use consistent hashing.
- **"Longer TTL is always better."** More staleness and bigger avalanches — add jitter.
